Radio promotion glossary40+ terms

By the RadioReach team Updated August 18, 2026 6 min read Reference & answers

Radio has a language of its own, and half of sounding professional is using it correctly. This glossary explains the terms independent artists actually run into while promoting music to radio — from adds and spins to NACC charts, mixshows, and one-sheets — in plain English. Terms are alphabetical, with cross-links to our deeper guides where they exist.

A

Add
When a station officially puts your song into its rotation. An add is the yes every radio campaign works toward — it means the station will actually play the track, not just consider it.
Airplay
Any broadcast of your music on a radio station. Confirmed airplay — spins you can verify in playlists or charts — is the currency of radio promotion.
Airplay monitoring
Services such as Nielsen BDSradio and Mediabase that detect broadcasts across stations and power commercial chart data. College and community airplay is mostly tracked by stations self-reporting playlists instead.
Americana
A roots-music format spanning country, folk, blues, and singer-songwriter material. Americana radio is largely noncommercial, programmer-driven, and notably open to independent artists; the Americana Music Association publishes the format's weekly airplay chart.

C

Chart reporting
The weekly process by which stations report their adds, playlists, and spins to chart aggregators. Airplay at reporting stations is what moves releases up genre charts.
College radio
Student-run (often community-supported) campus stations. The most accessible broadcast tier for independent artists: named music and genre directors, published submission processes, and chart reporting through organizations like NACC.
Community radio
Locally owned, volunteer-driven stations, often noncommercial. Community programmers choose their own music, host genre shows, and are reliably open to direct artist pitches that fit their programs.
Commercial radio
For-profit stations whose programming is ratings- and revenue-driven. Playlists at major commercial stations are tightly researched and rarely accept unsolicited music — the reason independent campaigns target other tiers first.

D

Daypart
A block of the broadcast day (mornings, middays, evenings) with its own audience and format expectations. Specialty and mix programming usually lives at night, when programmers have the most freedom.
Drive time
Morning and evening commutes — the most-listened (and most valuable) dayparts. Realistic expectation for a new artist: not drive time; a specialty show or overnight rotation is the realistic first win.
DJ / show host
The person on air. On community, college, and internet stations the host frequently chooses every track in their own show, which makes them a decision-maker worth pitching directly.

E

EPK (electronic press kit)
A single link holding everything a programmer or journalist needs: music, bio, photos, press, airplay history, and contact. See our guide to building an EPK for radio.

F

Format
A station's overall programming identity — Top 40, urban, country, Triple A, rock, news/talk. Matching your genre to station formats is step one of targeting.

G

Genre director
A station staff member (common at college stations) responsible for one genre's submissions and chart reporting — the single most relevant contact for many independent pitches.

I

Internet radio
Online-only stations and collectives, from global platforms to single-genre broadcasters. Streaming worldwide, DJ-curated, and typically the most receptive tier for independent submissions.

L

LPFM
Low-power FM: small, hyper-local noncommercial stations in the US. Tiny signals, but real community audiences and programmer autonomy — useful targets in your own town.

M

Market
A station's city or metro area. Radio promotion is organized market by market, and local relevance (hometown, tour stops) is one of the strongest pitch angles an artist has.
Mixshow
A DJ-hosted show — often late-night on urban, dance, and rhythmic stations — where new music traditionally breaks before formal playlisting. In hip-hop and dance, mixshow DJs are key gatekeepers.
Music director (MD)
The person at a college or community station who receives, screens, and adds new releases. For most independent artists, the MD is the single most important contact in radio.

N

NACC
The North American College and Community Radio collaboration — the charts college and community stations in the US and Canada report their airplay to, including genre charts. (Its predecessor, CMJ, was the earlier college-chart authority and is long dormant.)
Noncommercial radio
Stations without advertising-based licenses (community, college, public). Noncommercial programmers choose music with unusual freedom, which is why independent campaigns concentrate here.

O

One-sheet
The single-page PDF promoters and artists send with a release: art, facts, sound description, airplay history, links, and contact. The standard currency of radio pitching — see our EPK guide.

P

Payola rules
US law and FCC rules requiring disclosure of anything of value given in exchange for airplay. Practical upshot for artists: never pay for undisclosed spins, and treat anyone who sells guaranteed airplay as a liability.
Program director (PD)
The person responsible for a station's overall sound and schedule. At smaller stations the PD and MD are often the same person; at larger ones the PD is the final authority on adds.
Playlist log
A station's public record of what it played and when. Checking playlist logs is how independent artists confirm spins — and how they catch stations to thank.
Power rotation
The heaviest tier of spins a station gives a track. Reserved for a station's biggest priorities; reaching it as an outsider is rare by design.
Press release
A formatted announcement of a release or event sent to media. Useful for press, but radio pitching works better as short personal email than as press releases.
Promoter / plugger
A hired radio promotion professional who pitches your release to their station network and reports weekly on results. Costs vary widely by format and campaign length — see our DIY-vs-promoter comparison.
Public radio
Noncommercial, listener-supported stations and networks. Music-heavy public stations and their genre programs are meaningful targets for Americana, jazz, classical, and eclectic artists.

R

Radio edit
A version of your song prepared for broadcast: shortened structure and clean lyrics. Sending the album version to broadcast stations is one of the fastest ways to get skipped.
Record pool
A subscription service distributing tracks to working club and radio DJs. In hip-hop and dance, pool support generates the early DJ momentum programmers look for.
Rotation
The recurring schedule a station gives an added track — light, medium, or heavy — determining how often it plays. Most independent adds start in specialty shows or light rotation.

S

Satellite radio
National subscription radio. Some channels program independent music in specific genres; submissions typically run through label and promoter channels.
Simulcast
One station broadcasting another's signal (an HD subchannel or translator relaying a bigger station). If you get played on the source station, simulcast reach comes along with it.
Specialty show
A genre- or scene-focused program inside a broader station — a weekly metal, jazz, hip-hop, or local-music hour. Specialty shows are the most pitchable destination in all of radio for independent artists.
Spin
One broadcast play of your song. Spins (not adds alone) are how airplay is counted and charted.
Station ID
The legal on-air identification of a station (call letters, frequency, city). Unrelated promo tip: recorded station IDs by artists are a small currency of goodwill at community stations.
Syndication
A show distributed to multiple affiliate stations. One syndicated program can mean spins in dozens of markets from a single host relationship.

T

Tour support
Airplay coordinated with your tour dates in each market. One of the most effective campaign structures — programmers respond to music they can connect to a live date.
Translator
A small repeater transmitter that rebroadcasts a station in another area. Many community and noncommercial signals reach their cities through translators.
Triple A (adult album alternative)
A broad, album-oriented format — the natural radio home for singer-songwriter, indie, and roots artists, and the crossover target for Americana records.

U

Underwriting
Noncommercial radio's version of sponsorship: on-air acknowledgments that fund stations. Underwriting acknowledgments are how many college and community stations survive — and why their music programming stays independent.

Definitions describe common industry usage; individual stations and organizations may use terms slightly differently. See something missing? The glossary grows with our resource library.

Frequently asked questions

What's the difference between an add and a spin?

An add is the station's decision to put your song into rotation; a spin is each individual play after that. Charts are built from spins at reporting stations, so an add with no spins is a launch, not a result.

Who should I contact first at a radio station?

In order: the genre director for your style if one exists, then the music director, then the specialty-show host your music fits, then the program director. The Radio Reach Vault lists station contacts by role so you can skip the guessing.
